# General

- Page: <https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/NRES-746/Week1_IntroAndAlgorithms.html>.
  Open it before class; the three widgets need no internet once loaded.
- For live demos, run the matching section of
  `CODE_Week1_IntroAndAlgorithms.R` (same seeds, same numbers). The
  100,000-sample salmon loop takes under a second.
- Zoom the browser to 125-150% for the projector.
- Questions on the page have no answers. Answers are below; *Land:* is
  where discussion should end up.
- Readings for Canvas: Bolker ch. 1 (printed pp. 1-35; 1.3.2 on p. 9 is
  the analytical vs. computational distinction) and appendix A
  (A.1-A.4, pp. 480-482). The schedule also lists ch. 2-3.
- WODs: *Math & Stats Self-Diagnostic* (Monday) and *Pseudocoding a
  Permutation Test* (Wednesday), keys in `wod/answer_keys/`. Both are
  worked on the page (`#wod-diagnostic`, `#wod-permutation`).
- Lab 1 Act answers stay off the page. The lab section avoids the
  linearization of $ae^{-bx}$ (Act 2, 1c), the Ricker derivative and
  critical point (Act 2, Part 2), the 0-to-2 ramp (Act 2, Part 3), and
  SSR (Act 3). Its examples use different functions and numbers: a
  power law, $x^2e^{-x}$, a 0-to-4 ramp over 5 days.

# Part 1: What this course is about (Monday, ~15-20 min after the syllabus)

**Big picture (~5 min)**

- Walk the workflow left to right: problem first, then theories, then
  models (function + noise), fit, compare, revise. Point out where the
  semester's topics sit (functions, probability, simulation =
  MODELS; likelihood, Bayes, MCMC = FIT; AIC, CV = COMPARE).
- "Playing" with data, models, and probability: simulate from your own
  model and see if you can recover the parameters.

**How the course runs (~3 min)**

- WOD routine, Acts (alone, then group; wrong first attempts are
  expected), final project pitches, AI policy (closed in class unless a
  handout says otherwise), "stop me if it doesn't make sense."

**WOD (~10 min, including the neighbor comparison)**

- Answers: $x = 5$; $r = \ln(5.5)/8 = 0.213$; $f'(x) = 5(4x^2-3x)^4(8x-3)$,
  $f'(1) = 25$; $R(t) = 2t^2$, total 50; $P(A \cup B) = 0.7$; two
  children 1/3; CI (b); p-value (b); `site_data[, 2]`;
  `for (i in seq_along(values))`; braces around the function body.
- Collect the sheets and look at the self-ratings before Lab 1. Low
  calculus ratings mean more time on the lab's derivative section.

**Discussion (~3-5 min)**

- Q1 (CI of 0.42 to 0.61, "95% chance the truth is in there") *Land:*
  strictly, the 95% belongs to the procedure: in repeated samples, 95%
  of such intervals cover the true value; this one either does or
  doesn't. A Bayesian credible interval does carry that reading (given
  a prior), which comes later in the semester. For most management
  decisions the distinction doesn't change the action; it matters when
  someone treats the interval's ends as hard limits.
- Q2 (your own problem and two theories) *Land:* open. Push for a
  problem stated as a decision or need, and for theories that predict
  different data; if they predict the same data, no study separates
  them.

# Part 2: Math tools for Lab 1 (lab opening, ~10-15 min)

- A refresher, not a first lesson. Do logs and the product + chain
  rules; skim integration if time is short (Act 2 Part 3 gives a worked
  constant-rate example on the handout).
- **Board:** exponent rules, then logs as "what power?"; the growing
  square, then the rectangle.
- Q (power law: rise per tenfold mass; slope of 1) *Land:* 0.75 per
  decade (0.477, 1.227, 1.977, 2.727). A slope of 1 means rate is
  proportional to mass, so the rate per gram is constant; a slope of
  0.75 means larger animals use less energy per gram.
- **Widget (growing rectangle):** square mode, $x = 3$. At $dx = 1.5$:
  exact change 11.25, strips 9, corner 2.25 (20%). At $dx = 0.1$: exact
  0.61, strips 0.60, corner 0.01 (1.6%). Ask for a prediction before
  sliding. Then rectangle mode: shrink $h$ and watch the corner share go
  to 0.
- Q (corner's share; why drop it) *Land:* the share is $dx/(2x + dx)$,
  which goes to 0. Divided by $dx$, the corner contributes $dx$, which
  vanishes in the limit, so it doesn't affect the derivative. The exact
  new area still includes it.
- $x^2 e^{-x}$: $f' = x(2-x)e^{-x}$, critical points 0 and 2. This is
  the closest parallel to point stuck groups toward in Act 2 Part 2,
  without giving the Ricker answer.
- **Widget (accumulation):** start with the constant rate (any rule is
  exact, area 10). Ramp, left edge, 5 rectangles: 8; right edge: 12;
  midpoint: 10. Rise-and-fall, left edge, 5 rectangles: 6.38 vs. 7.13
  exact; midpoint 7.24. Slide to 100 rectangles.
- Q (left/right/midpoint on the ramp) *Land:* the ramp increases, so the
  left edge takes the lowest height in each slice (too small) and the
  right edge the highest (too big). For a straight line, the midpoint's
  overshoot on one half of each slice exactly cancels the undershoot on
  the other; a curved function doesn't cancel.
- Circulating: Act 1 and Act 3 need none of this. Act 2 Part 1 needs
  log rules; Part 2 product + chain; Part 3 "area = total."

# Part 3: Algorithms for inference (Wednesday, ~32 min)

**Big picture (~3 min)**

- COMPARE box, simplest version: data vs. a null model. Analytical
  (formula, exact, needs assumptions) vs. computational (a program,
  approximate, needs only the story). Bolker 1.3.2.

**WOD (~6 min)**

- Statistic: difference in means, $174.8 - 178.2 = -3.4$ g. Two-tailed
  (no direction predicted). Pseudocode: shuffle labels, recompute,
  store, compare. Have a couple of students read their steps aloud
  before showing the page's list; the R version waits for section 4.

**Two routes to a z-test (~10 min)**

- $\bar{x} = 3.476$, $SE = 0.285$, $z = -3.60$, $p = 0.00016$.
- Simulation: 21 of 100,000 means at or below 3.476, $p \approx
  0.00021$. SD of simulated means 0.286 vs. $SE = 0.285$: the loop finds
  the standard error without the formula.
- **Board pseudocode:** simulate a sample under the null, compute its
  mean, store; repeat; p = fraction at least as extreme.
- One-tailed here vs. two-tailed for the lizards; worth a check-in.

**Permutation test (~10 min)**

- $p \approx 0.37$ (seed 746); t-test 0.36. Not significant, a useful
  contrast with the salmon.
- Put the page's loop next to the WOD's fill-in skeleton.
- **Widget (resampling):** lizards first, 10,000 replicates (about
  0.37, the shaded tails on both sides). Then salmon: add 1,000 at a
  time; most runs show 0 extreme means. Ask what p to report before
  answering.
- Q (salmon runs of 1,000 with no extreme means) *Land:* report
  $p < 0.001$ (at most 1 in 1,000), not $p = 0$. With true $p =
  0.00016$, 1,000 replicates expect 0.16 hits, so about 85% of runs show
  none. Seeing about 5 takes roughly 30,000 replicates; the page's
  100,000 gave 21.
- `permutation_test()`: packaging the loop. Skip if behind.

**Discussion (~3-5 min)**

- Q1 (formula 0.00016 vs. simulation 0.00021) *Land:* the simulation's
  own standard error is about $\sqrt{p(1-p)/N} = 0.00004$, so they agree
  within noise. Trust the formula when its assumptions hold (here they
  are given); trust the simulation when the formula's assumptions fail
  or no formula exists, and add replicates until the noise is small
  relative to the decision.
- Q2 (when permutation and t-tests disagree) *Land:* small samples
  with strong skew or an outlier (the t-test leans on normality of the
  mean), or very unequal spreads. The permutation test assumes only
  that labels are exchangeable under the null, so it holds up there.
- Q3 (own research) *Land:* open. The random step is whatever the null
  says is arbitrary: labels, locations, timing, or draws from a
  simulated process.

**Bonus (cut first): bootstrap**

- $R^2$: girth 0.94, height 0.36. 95% bootstrap intervals: girth 0.90
  to 0.96, height 0.14 to 0.59. Third flavor of the same loop
  (resample rows with replacement). Lab 2 Act 3 uses a bootstrap, so
  don't work its example here.
